newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG begins "horse-trading" for next government.
newsitem.headline: PNG begins "horse-trading" for next government.

text.p: The Papua New Guinea government of Sir Julius Chan was dissolved on Tuesday with the return of writs in the national election, heralding a week of tough political "horse-trading" to form the next government.

Sir Michael Somare, the South Pacific nation's first prime minister, said he was confident he would be the country's next leader, heading a coalition government based mainly on his cross-party National Alliance group and independents.
Somare said the election had shown people wanted a change in leadership. "Now we need to form a government that will reunite PNG and give confidence back to the people," he told Reuters.

"Ours is a collective leadership and I have around me some very experienced leaders and former senior public servants and community leaders. The group is made up of like-minded people who want the best for this country."

Outgoing prime minister Chan, who lost his seat in a shock voter backlash against his hiring of African mercenaries to end the seccessionist revolt on Bougainville, said he hoped his party could still form a government.
Chan's People's Progressive Party (PPP) and outgoing deputy prime minister Chris Haiveta's Pangu party both polled well, winning 16 and 15 seats respectively in the 109-seat parliament.
But many senior PPP and Pangu members lost their seats in the mercenary backlash and political analysts doubt Haiveta can duplicate Chan's unifying force.
Local newspapers have reported that former prime minister and senior Pangu member Sir Rabbie Namaliu may split with his party and side with Somare.

However, Haiveta, who was criticised by a judicial inquiry into the failed US$36 million mercenary deal, which he was heavily involved in negotiating, remains confident. The mercenary deal led to a dangerous army revolt which only ended when Chan and Haiveta stepped aside.

"Irrespective of the media hype, the party is solid and is in a coalition with PPP and other like-minded parties and we will stay on in government," Haiveta told The Post-Courier newspaper on Tuesday.

Another group that could decide the outcome is former deputy prime minister Ted Diro's People's Action Party. Diro, according to analysts, holds a certain magnetism over independents and has publicly said he wants to be prime minister.
A record 36 independents have been elected, but analysts say the outgoing coalition would find it difficult to attract them to form a government as most had campaigned for change.

"The race for the top post appears likely to be between Sir Michael and Mr Diro, but the horse-trading will finally determine the outcome," said political scientist Ray Anere of the University of Papua New Guinea.

But analysts wared that PNG's multi-party system, and the fact that less than one-third of the 2,370 candidates ran on a party ticket, still made it difficult to predict who would form the next government.

"Intense lobbying will continue until parliament sits next week. Experience has shown that even when parliament resumes, there may be members crossing the floor to sway the results," said one political analyst.
Parliament will sit next Tuesday for the election of a speaker, followed by the formation of a government by the group that has the largest numbers.
